memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: So the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh left the Israelites at Shiloh in Canaan to return to Gilead, their own land, which they had acquired in accordance with the command of the Lord through Moses. When they came to Geliloth near the Jordan in the land of Canaan, the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh built an imposing altar there by the Jordan. — Josh 22:9-10 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
On their way home, the eastern tribes stop by the Jordan and build a large, striking altar. To us, reading quickly, it might seem a natural act of worship. But this simple sentence is about to set off a crisis, because in Israel there was to be only one place of sacrifice — the tabernacle. A second altar could look like rival worship, even rebellion against the Lord.

The tribes had good intentions, as we will soon see. But their action, without explanation, was open to serious misunderstanding. What they meant for unity looked, from a distance, like division.

There is a lesson here for all of us. Even sincere hearts can act in ways that confuse or alarm others. Good intentions are not always enough; how our actions appear to our brothers and sisters matters too. Paul urged believers to be careful not to cause others to stumble, and to do what leads to peace (Rom 14:19).

Before the crisis unfolds, pause and notice the tension. God cares about pure worship, and He also cares about how His people relate to one another. As we will see, this near-disaster becomes a story of grace. But it begins with a reminder to consider not only our own intentions, but how our actions land on those around us.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Have your good intentions ever been misunderstood by others?
2. Do you consider how your actions might appear to fellow believers?
3. How can you pursue both faithfulness to God and peace with others?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord, help me to act with pure intentions and also with wisdom, considering how my actions affect others. Make me a peacemaker among Your people. Amen.
